nodes.label: Tughril Beg founds the sultanate
nodes.full: Tughril Beg led his Oghuz Turkic followers from Central Asia through Khorasan to Baghdad, where the Abbasid caliph invested him with the title Sultan in 1055 — the first time the caliphate formally recognised a single military ruler as supreme temporal authority over the whole Sunni Islamic world, ending the Buyid amirate in the same stroke.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on Tughril Beg's entry into Baghdad and investiture.

nodes.label: Tughril enters Baghdad
nodes.full: Tughril Beg's entry into Baghdad, ostensibly to rescue the caliph from a rebellious Turkic general, ended Buyid control of the city and installed the Seljuks as the new military power behind the Abbasid throne — a change of guard for the caliphate's protector-dynasty rather than any change in the caliph's own powerless status.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on the Seljuk entry into Baghdad.

nodes.label: Sunni revival
nodes.full: Seljuk sultans and Nizam al-Mulk deliberately promoted Sunni orthodoxy — particularly through the Nizamiyya madrasas' curriculum — as an ideological counterweight to both the Shia Buyid legacy they had displaced and the Ismaili challenge growing at Alamut, a state-sponsored religious project as much political as theological in its aims.
nodes.src: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama, on the explicitly anti-Ismaili and pro-Sunni aims of his religious policy.

nodes.label: Alp Arslan
nodes.full: Alp Arslan's decisive defeat and capture of the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes at Manzikert in 1071 shattered Byzantine defensive capacity in eastern Anatolia — opening the region to Turkic migration and settlement on a scale that would permanently reshape Anatolia's demographic and political future.
nodes.src: Michael Attaleiates, History (Byzantine eyewitness account); Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh.

nodes.label: Battle of Manzikert
nodes.full: Alp Arslan's army defeated and captured the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV at Manzikert — treated with notable clemency by Alp Arslan himself — but the political chaos the defeat triggered at Constantinople did far more lasting damage to Byzantine Anatolia than the battle's own casualties, opening the region to unchecked Turkic migration for a generation afterward.
nodes.src: Michael Attaleiates, History; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh.

nodes.label: Turkic settlement of Anatolia
nodes.full: In the decades following Manzikert, Turkic pastoralist tribes migrated into Anatolia in numbers far beyond what any single battle's aftermath could explain — a sustained demographic movement that would, over the following two centuries, transform Anatolia from a predominantly Greek Christian Byzantine province into the Turkish-speaking Muslim heartland from which the Ottoman Empire would eventually emerge.
nodes.src: Speros Vryonis, The Decline of Medieval Hellenism in Asia Minor (1971), on the post-Manzikert Turkic settlement of Anatolia.

nodes.label: Manzikert chain of consequences
nodes.full: Manzikert's political aftermath in Byzantium — a succession crisis that left the empire unable to defend Anatolia — is what later prompted Byzantine appeals to the West that helped trigger the First Crusade in 1095, and set in motion the centuries-long process by which Anatolia would become permanently Turkish, culminating eventually in the rise of the Ottoman state.
nodes.src: Comparative Byzantine-Seljuk political history, on Manzikert's cascading long-term consequences.

nodes.label: Malik-Shah and Nizam al-Mulk
nodes.full: Malik-Shah's reign, guided for three decades by his formidable Persian vizier Nizam al-Mulk, marked the Seljuk sultanate's territorial and administrative peak — a partnership so effective that its end, with vizier and sultan both dead within weeks of each other in 1092, precipitated the sultanate's rapid fragmentation.
nodes.src: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on the 1092 double death.

nodes.label: Nizamiyya madrasas
nodes.full: Nizam al-Mulk endowed a network of state-funded Sunni religious colleges (madrasas) across the sultanate's major cities, standardising advanced religious and legal education and training the administrators and jurists who staffed his own bureaucracy — an institutional model for state-sponsored higher education that spread across the wider Islamic world for centuries.
nodes.src: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama; George Makdisi, The Rise of Colleges (1981), on the Nizamiyya system.

nodes.label: Scholars in the Nizamiyya network
nodes.full: The Nizamiyya madrasas at Baghdad, Nishapur, Isfahan and elsewhere formed a connected network across which scholars, texts and legal opinions moved with unusual freedom for the era — the theologian al-Ghazali's own career, teaching at the Baghdad Nizamiyya before a celebrated spiritual crisis and retreat, exemplifies the intellectual mobility the system enabled.
nodes.src: al-Ghazali, al-Munqidh min al-Dalal (Deliverance from Error), on his own Nizamiyya teaching career.

nodes.label: Khayyam and the Jalali calendar
nodes.full: Malik-Shah commissioned the poet-mathematician-astronomer Omar Khayyam to lead a team reforming the solar calendar, producing the Jalali calendar — more astronomically accurate over the long run than the Gregorian calendar that would not exist for another five centuries — while Khayyam's other work in algebra classified and solved cubic equations geometrically.
nodes.src: Omar Khayyam's own astronomical and mathematical treatises; the Jalali calendar's continued partial use in modern Iran and Afghanistan.

nodes.label: Siyasatnama
nodes.full: Written for Malik-Shah near the end of his own life, the Siyasatnama ('Book of Government') laid out Nizam al-Mulk's theory of just and effective kingship through historical example and practical advice — one of the most influential works of Persian political theory, read and imitated by rulers and administrators for centuries after the Seljuk state it was written to serve had disappeared.
nodes.src: Nizam al-Mulk, Siyasatnama (Siyar al-Muluk).

nodes.label: Isfahan dome chambers
nodes.full: Nizam al-Mulk and his rival vizier Taj al-Mulk each sponsored one of two great brick dome chambers added to Isfahan's congregational mosque, their sophisticated squinch-and-muqarnas construction solving the geometric problem of setting a round dome over a square room with an elegance still studied by architectural historians as a high point of Islamic engineering.
nodes.src: Masjed-e Jāmé of Isfahan, extant structure, UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 2012).

nodes.label: Unified plateau commerce
nodes.full: Malik-Shah's reign briefly reunified nearly the whole Iranian plateau and much of the Fertile Crescent under a single political authority for the first time since the Abbasid caliphate's own early centuries — a political unity that measurably lowered the transaction costs of long-distance trade across a region more often divided among rival, mutually taxing powers.
nodes.src: Comparative economic geography of the Great Seljuk sultanate at its territorial peak.

nodes.label: Caravanserai network
nodes.full: Seljuk sultans and their viziers sponsored the construction of a dense network of fortified roadside inns (caravanserais) spaced roughly a day's journey apart across the plateau's major trade routes, dramatically improving the safety and speed of long-distance commercial and pilgrim travel.
nodes.src: Surviving Seljuk-era caravanserai remains across the Iranian plateau; comparative infrastructure history.

nodes.label: Nizari state at Alamut
nodes.full: Hassan-i Sabbah seized the mountain fortress of Alamut in 1090 and built a network of similarly fortified strongholds into a genuinely independent Nizari Ismaili state within Seljuk territory, defended less by conventional armies than by a doctrine of targeted assassination of hostile political and religious leaders — the origin, via medieval European garbling of 'Hashishin,' of the English word 'assassin.'
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh; Marshall Hodgson, The Order of Assassins (1955).

nodes.label: Assassination as a weapon of the weak
nodes.full: The Nizari Ismaili state at Alamut never fielded an army capable of meeting the Seljuk sultanate in open battle, and instead relied on the targeted killing of specific hostile officials and rulers — a documented case of a small, doctrinally marginalised religious community adopting an asymmetric political tactic precisely because conventional military and political power was closed to it.
nodes.src: Marshall Hodgson, The Order of Assassins (1955), on the strategic logic of Nizari political violence.

nodes.label: Nizam al-Mulk assassinated
nodes.full: A member of the Nizari Ismaili movement, disguised as a Sufi petitioner, stabbed Nizam al-Mulk to death — the first prominent victim of what would become a sustained Nizari campaign of targeted political killing, and a loss from which the Seljuk administrative machine never fully recovered.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, on the assassination and its attribution to the Nizaris.

nodes.label: Fragmentation after Malik-Shah
nodes.full: Rival sons and regional atabegs (Turkic military guardians originally appointed to protect young Seljuk princes) carved the sultanate into competing power centres across Iran, Iraq and Syria — the atabegs increasingly ruling in their princely wards' names while accumulating genuinely independent authority of their own.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on the succession wars following Malik-Shah's death.

nodes.label: Seljuk succession wars
nodes.full: Malik-Shah's sons and their atabeg guardians fought a prolonged, multi-sided civil war for control of the sultanate's core territories, permanently fracturing what had briefly been a unified Seljuk realm into the separate eastern (Khorasan) and western (Iraq-Iran) sultanates that would never again be reunited.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on the succession wars of the 1090s and 1100s.

nodes.label: Atabeg system
nodes.full: Turkic military commanders appointed as atabegs — guardians and tutors to young Seljuk princes given nominal provincial governorships — increasingly exercised the real power of the offices they formally only administered on a minor's behalf, a delegation of authority that repeatedly slid into outright independent atabeg dynasties across Iran, Iraq and Syria.
nodes.src: Comparative institutional analysis of the Seljuk atabeg system and its successor states.

nodes.label: Iqta land grants
nodes.full: Seljuk administration relied heavily on iqta grants — assigning military commanders the tax revenue of a specified territory in lieu of a salary paid from the central treasury — a fiscal-military system that reduced the state's own cash-handling burden but steadily strengthened provincial commanders' independent power at the centre's expense.
nodes.src: Ann Lambton, on the iqta system's development under the Great Seljuks.

nodes.label: Fragmentation into atabeg states
nodes.full: By the early 13th century the once-unified Great Seljuk sultanate survived only as a patchwork of regional atabeg successor states and, finally, the briefly dominant but shallow-rooted Khwarazmian empire — a fragmentation pattern that would leave the whole region catastrophically unprepared for the single unified threat the Mongols were about to pose.
nodes.src: Comparative political geography of the post-Seljuk Iranian plateau on the eve of the Mongol invasions.

nodes.label: Sanjar
nodes.full: Sanjar held the eastern Seljuk sultanate together from Merv for nearly four decades, the last ruler able to claim genuine authority over the dynasty's original Khorasan heartland, before Ghuzz Turkic tribesmen he had settled as frontier auxiliaries revolted, sacked Merv, and held him captive for several humiliating years until his death.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on Sanjar's reign and captivity.

nodes.label: Ghuzz revolt and Merv sacked
nodes.full: Ghuzz Turkic tribes Sanjar had settled as frontier guards in Khorasan revolted, defeated his army, and sacked Merv itself — one of the great cities of the Islamic world — before holding the aged sultan captive for roughly three years, a humiliating collapse of central authority from which the eastern Seljuk sultanate never recovered.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi'l-Tarikh, on the Ghuzz revolt and the sack of Merv.

nodes.label: Khwarazmian rise
nodes.full: Originally Seljuk-appointed governors of Khwarazm, the Khwarazm-Shahs expanded rapidly into the power vacuum left by Sanjar's death, briefly building an empire stretching across most of Iran and Central Asia — a state whose sudden vast extent and shallow administrative roots would prove catastrophically unable to withstand the Mongol invasion beginning in 1219.
nodes.src: al-Nasawi, Sirat al-Sultan Jalal al-Din Mankubirti, on the rise of the Khwarazmian state.

nodes.label: Battle of Qatwan
nodes.full: On 9 September 1141 the Qara Khitai, a steppe empire from the east, crushed Sultan Sanjar’s Seljuk army and its Karakhanid vassals on the Qatwan steppe north of Samarkand, after the Karakhanid ruler appealed to Sanjar for protection. Sanjar escaped with a handful of horsemen and the Seljuks lost control of Transoxiana — a blow from which Seljuk power in the east, already stretched, did not recover.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi al-Ta’rikh, and Juvayni on the battle; the date of 9 September 1141 follows standard accounts; medieval figures for the armies and the losses are unreliable and not given here.

nodes.label: The Ghurids
nodes.full: The Ghurids of the central Afghan highlands, under the brothers Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad and Mu’izz al-Din Muhammad, held Ghazni and Herat by 1175, annexed the Ghaznavid principality of Lahore in 1186, and after a defeat at Taraori in 1191 won the second Battle of Tarain in 1192, opening northern India to their commanders. At its height the realm reached from Khorasan to Bengal; after Mu’izz al-Din’s death it fragmented, and the Khwarazm-Shah Muhammad II annexed its remaining lands by 1215.
nodes.src: Minhaj-i Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri, the principal Persian history of the Ghurids; Encyclopaedia Iranica and Britannica entries on Mu’izz al-Din Muhammad ibn Sam; the dates follow standard reference accounts.

nodes.label: Sanjar mausoleum at Merv
nodes.full: Sultan Sanjar’s mausoleum at Merv, the Seljuk capital in the east, is a square domed hall about 27 metres on a side with a dome rising some 38 metres, once faced in turquoise tile, and built in the mid-12th century in the lifetime of the last great Seljuk ruler, who died in 1157. The city around it was devastated by the Mongols in 1221, but the tomb survives as the best-preserved monument of Seljuk Merv.
nodes.src: The Sanjar mausoleum, part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of Ancient Merv; construction dates (c.1152–1157) follow standard references and the dome height varies slightly between sources.

nodes.label: Minaret of Jam
nodes.full: A 65-metre baked-brick minaret, rising from an octagonal base in a remote river valley of the central Afghan highlands and covered in bands of Kufic and Naskh calligraphy, geometric patterns and Quranic verses, was built about 1194 under the Ghurid sultan Ghiyath al-Din. It is the finest surviving monument of the Ghurid state; it has been on UNESCO’s List of World Heritage in Danger since 2002 because of erosion and a lack of active conservation.
nodes.src: UNESCO World Heritage Site no. 211, Minaret and Archaeological Remains of Jam; the date c.1194 follows the minaret’s own inscriptions as read in standard references, and the site’s identification with the Ghurid capital Firuzkuh is probable but not certain.

nodes.label: Sana’i and Attar
nodes.full: Sana’i of Ghazna completed the Hadiqat al-haqiqa, the first major Persian mystical epic, in 1131 under the Ghaznavids, and Farid al-Din Attar of Nishapur composed the Conference of the Birds in 1177, an allegory of the soul’s journey in which the birds seek their king, the Simorgh. Between them the eastern cities fixed the form of the Persian Sufi poem that Rumi later drew on.
nodes.src: Sana’i, Hadiqat al-haqiqa (completed 1131); Attar, Mantiq al-tayr (Conference of the Birds, dated 1177); the dates are conventional and some scholars place Attar’s poem a little later.

nodes.label: Abdullah Ansari of Herat
nodes.full: Abdullah Ansari (1006–1089), a Hanbali jurist and Sufi preacher of Herat, wrote in Persian as well as Arabic, and his Munajat, a set of intimate prayers, is counted among the finest works of Persian devotional prose. His teaching and shrine made Herat a lasting centre of Sunni Sufi devotion in the eastern Islamic world.
nodes.src: Abdullah Ansari, Munajat-nama and Tabaqat al-Sufiyya (Persian recension of his teaching); the attribution of some works to Ansari himself, as opposed to his students, is debated.

nodes.label: Qara Khitai advance into Transoxiana
nodes.full: A steppe empire from the east whose advance threatens the Karakhanid vassals of the Seljuks and draws Sanjar into the field.
nodes.src: named in this folio’s c6
